topic: Evidence on time-restricted eating (intermittent fasting) versus continuous calorie restriction for weight loss and metabolic health

key_points.point: A 2026 Cochrane review (22 RCTs, 1,995 adults) found intermittent fasting no better than regular dietary advice such as continuous restriction: weight difference -0.33% (95% CI -0.92 to 0.26), low certainty.

atoms.fact: A 2026 Cochrane review (22 RCTs, 1,995 adults) found intermittent fasting no better than regular dietary advice such as continuous restriction.
The 2026 Cochrane review found a weight difference of -0.33% (95% CI -0.92 to 0.26) between intermittent fasting and regular dietary advice, with low certainty.

key_points.point: The 12-month NEJM trial (139 adults) found calorie restriction plus 8am-4pm eating gave -8.0 kg versus -6.3 kg with calorie restriction alone, a non-significant difference; calorie deficit drove most benefit.

atoms.fact: The 12-month NEJM trial of time-restricted eating (139 adults) found calorie restriction plus 8am-4pm eating gave -8.0 kg versus -6.3 kg with calorie restriction alone, a non-significant difference.
In the 12-month NEJM trial of time-restricted eating, calorie deficit drove most of the benefit.

key_points.point: Lowe et al. (JAMA Intern Med 2020, 116 adults, 12 weeks) found 16:8 TRE did not beat consistent three-meal timing for weight (between-group -0.26 kg, P=.63) or most metabolic markers.

atoms.fact: Lowe et al. (JAMA Intern Med 2020, 116 adults, 12 weeks) found 16:8 TRE did not beat consistent three-meal timing for weight (between-group -0.26 kg, P=.63).
Lowe et al. found 16:8 TRE did not beat consistent three-meal timing for most metabolic markers.

key_points.point: An umbrella review/network meta-analysis (BMC Med 2024; 153 studies, 9,846 people) found direct TRE vs continuous energy restriction weight difference -2.41 kg (CI -5.14 to 0.33), non-significant; most direct evidence was low or very low quality.

atoms.fact: An umbrella review/network meta-analysis (BMC Med 2024; 153 studies, 9,846 people) found direct TRE vs continuous energy restriction weight difference of -2.41 kg (CI -5.14 to 0.33), non-significant.
In the BMC Med 2024 umbrella review/network meta-analysis, most direct evidence on TRE versus continuous energy restriction was low or very low quality.

key_points.point: A JAMA Netw Open 2024 meta-analysis (29 RCTs, 2,485 adults, 12+ weeks) found TRE lowered weight by 1.37 kg (CI -1.99 to -0.75) versus controls; authors called this small, of uncertain clinical importance, and low certainty.

atoms.fact: A JAMA Netw Open 2024 meta-analysis (29 RCTs, 2,485 adults, 12+ weeks) found TRE lowered weight by 1.37 kg (CI -1.99 to -0.75) versus controls.
The authors of the JAMA Netw Open 2024 TRE meta-analysis called the weight effect small, of uncertain clinical importance, and low certainty.

key_points.point: Energy intake reduction is the main driver: TRE trials show about 164 kcal/day lower intake, and a Nutrition Reviews meta-analysis found larger weight effects vs non-isocaloric controls (-2.82 kg) than isocaloric ones (-1.46 kg).

atoms.fact: Energy intake reduction is the main driver of weight loss with TRE.
TRE trials show about 164 kcal/day lower intake.
A Nutrition Reviews meta-analysis found larger TRE weight effects versus non-isocaloric controls (-2.82 kg) than isocaloric ones (-1.46 kg).

key_points.point: Metabolic benefits of TRE are modest: fasting glucose about -1.15 mg/dL and HbA1c -0.08% vs controls, with no significant change in LDL or blood pressure; TRE added to calorie restriction gave no extra BP, glucose or lipid benefit.

atoms.fact: The metabolic benefits of TRE are modest.
TRE lowered fasting glucose by about 1.15 mg/dL versus controls.
TRE lowered HbA1c by 0.08% versus controls.
TRE produced no significant change in LDL or blood pressure versus controls.
TRE added to calorie restriction gave no extra blood pressure, glucose or lipid benefit.

key_points.point: Adding TRE to calorie restriction gave a small extra weight reduction of about 1.4 kg (WMD -1.40, 95% CI -1.81 to -1.00; 8 trials, 579 adults) with low or very low certainty.

atoms.fact: Adding TRE to calorie restriction gave a small extra weight reduction of about 1.4 kg (WMD -1.40, 95% CI -1.81 to -1.00; 8 trials, 579 adults).
The evidence for an extra weight reduction from adding TRE to calorie restriction was of low or very low certainty.

key_points.point: Lean mass is a concern: pooled TRE trials show about 0.42 kg lean mass loss, and Lowe et al. found a greater appendicular lean mass index decrease with TRE than with regular meal timing.

atoms.fact: Lean mass is a concern with TRE.
Pooled TRE trials show about 0.42 kg lean mass loss.
Lowe et al. found a greater appendicular lean mass index decrease with TRE than with regular meal timing.

key_points.point: Versus no intervention, intermittent fasting gave -3.42% weight change (moderate certainty), but Cochrane authors judged this unlikely to be clinically meaningful; safety and quality-of-life data were sparse and inconsistently reported.

atoms.fact: In the Cochrane review, intermittent fasting versus no intervention gave -3.42% weight change (moderate certainty).
The Cochrane authors judged the weight effect of intermittent fasting versus no intervention unlikely to be clinically meaningful.
In the Cochrane review, safety and quality-of-life data on intermittent fasting were sparse and inconsistently reported.

key_points.point: Evidence limits: trials are short (mostly under 12-16 months), small, heterogeneous in eating windows, often high risk of bias, and unrepresentative (NEJM trial mean age about 32); long-term sustainability and hard outcomes are unproven.

atoms.fact: TRE trials are short (mostly under 12-16 months).
TRE trials are small and heterogeneous in eating windows.
TRE trials are often at high risk of bias.
TRE trials are unrepresentative (the NEJM trial's mean age was about 32).
Long-term sustainability and hard outcomes of TRE are unproven.
